analysis.one_liner: Treats super PAC spending coordinated with a candidate as a campaign contribution, with penalties.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced and sent to committee in January 2015 but never got a hearing or vote before the 114th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current law, super PACs can raise unlimited money and spend it on elections as long as they act independently of the candidate. This bill would tighten that rule: any spending a super PAC plans with a candidate's campaign, or any ad using material the campaign produced, would count as a campaign contribution subject to normal limits. It would also bar federal candidates and officeholders from personally raising money for super PACs or other groups that ignore contribution limits. The bill never received a committee hearing or floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary voters, in two ways. First, the bill narrows the loophole that lets candidates effectively direct unlimited outside money while formally staying uncoordinated, which increases the weight of ordinary small donations relative to large ones. Second, disclosure and contribution rules would apply to spending that is currently arranged behind the scenes, so voters would see who paid for ads a candidate helped design.

how_it_helps.text: Counts any payment for a coordinated expenditure — spending planned with a candidate, the candidate's committee, or their agents — as a campaign contribution subject to existing limits [S2][S3].

Defines coordination broadly enough to close common workarounds: it applies even if the super PAC set up internal 'firewalls' to hide information-sharing, and covers groups founded or managed by a candidate's former campaign staff or advisers, sharing donor lists, or using the candidate's campaign video or written material [S3].

Bars federal candidates and officeholders, their agents, and related entities from soliciting, receiving, directing, or transferring funds to or on behalf of any committee or 527 organization that accepts donations that do not comply with federal limits and reporting rules [S2][S3].
Imposes a penalty of up to 300% of the coordinated payment for knowing and willful violations, with officers and directors jointly liable if the penalty goes unpaid [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Super PACs and their major donors, who would lose the ability to spend unlimited amounts on ads built around a candidate's own strategy and material. Candidates and their campaigns would lose the ability to use outside groups to raise unlimited money beyond contribution limits.
analysis.who_pays_short: Super PACs and their large donors

drawbacks.text: It would loosen an important protection for free speech and issue advocacy: the CRS summary notes the bill removes a provision the Supreme Court in McConnell v. FEC had struck down as unconstitutional, and an expanded definition of coordination that covers ads merely 'promoting' or 'attacking' a candidate during a 60- or 120-day window could sweep in some genuinely independent speech and chill participation by outside groups [S2][S3].

Some coordination concerns could be addressed by FEC regulation or disclosure rules rather than a new statutory penalty structure, so the bill's sweeping definitions carry enforcement burden and constitutional risk [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core aim — stopping campaigns and super PACs from secretly operating as one entity while claiming independence — is widely understood to be a real loophole, and the bill's mechanics are targeted at the actual ways coordination happens today (shared consultants, donor lists, campaign video, firewalls). The main risk is overreach: definitions that reach ads that merely 'promote' a candidate could chill legitimate independent advocacy, and enforcement would fall to the FEC, which is often deadlocked. On balance the bill's benefits to voters outweigh its costs, though a narrower version might better survive legal challenge.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Committee on House Administration on January 21, 2015, and the committee never held a hearing or brought it to a vote before the 114th Congress ended in January 2017 [S5][S1].

narrative.text: The bill was introduced by Rep. David Price (D-NC) with Rep. Chris Van Hollen on January 21, 2015 and referred to the House Committee on House Administration [S3][S5].
That referral was the bill's only action; no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever occurred [S5].
It drew 12 cosponsors, 11 Democrats and 1 Republican, before the Congress ended [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Super PACs, their major donors, and the campaigns that benefit from coordinated outside spending are better off, since the coordination limits never became law and the legislation died without a vote.

sides.party_line_note: Support was almost entirely Democratic — 11 of 12 cosponsors were Democrats — and the Republican-controlled House committee never acted on the bill [S4][S1].

industries.industry: Super PACs and their major donors
industries.note: The bill would strip super PACs of the ability to run unlimited spending built around a candidate's own strategy and material, and would bar candidates from fundraising for them. Their loss of influence is the voters' gain in accountability, since coordinated spending would once again be subject to contribution limits and disclosure.

industries.industry: Political consulting and campaign media firms
industries.note: The bill restricts a consultant shared between a campaign and an outside group from serving both, cutting off a lucrative dual-client model for the largest firms, while firms that keep separate engagements for separate clients lose little.

Groups organized under Section 527 that accept unlimited donations could no longer receive solicited or directed funds from federal candidates and officeholders, closing another channel for influence beyond contribution limits.
